title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Renal artery stenosis (RAS) is defined by the narrowing of one or both renal arteries and represents an important, potentially reversible cause of secondary hypertension and progressive kidney dysfunction. Atherosclerotic disease accounts for the vast majority of cases, typically affecting older adults with generalized vascular disease, whereas fibromuscular dysplasia more commonly affects younger individuals. Less frequent causes include vasculitis, extrinsic compression, radiation injury, neurofibromatosis, and congenital anomalies. Reduced renal perfusion activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, contributing to hypertension, ischemic nephropathy, and eventual chronic kidney disease or end-stage renal disease. Although RAS accounts for a small proportion of overall hypertension cases, prevalence increases substantially among individuals with refractory or resistant hypertension, recurrent flash pulmonary edema, or unexplained renal dysfunction, underscoring the importance of timely recognition.

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This course strengthens clinicians' knowledge of the pathophysiology, clinical features, and diagnostic evaluation of RAS, with emphasis on the appropriate use of duplex ultrasonography, computed tomography angiography, and magnetic resonance angiography. Learners examine evidence-based approaches to medical management, patient selection for revascularization, and longitudinal monitoring of renal function and blood pressure control. Educational content highlights the value of collaboration among an interprofessional healthcare team, including nephrology, interventional cardiology, radiology, nursing, and vascular surgery. Coordinated communication and shared decision-making support accurate diagnosis, individualized treatment planning, and improved long-term outcomes for patients with renal artery stenosis.

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Apply evidence-based guidelines to the diagnostic evaluation and longitudinal management of atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis across diverse clinical presentations. Interpret diagnostic imaging and laboratory studies used in the evaluation of suspected renal artery stenosis. Identify high-risk clinical scenarios, such as recurrent flash pulmonary edema or progressive renal dysfunction, that warrant urgent escalation of care. Collaborate with interprofessional team members, including nephrologists, interventional cardiologists, radiologists, vascular surgeons and nurses to improve coordination, communication, and patient outcomes in the management of renal artery stenosis. title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Introduction
content: Renal artery stenosis (RAS) is typically defined as more than 60% narrowing of one or both renal arteries and is a major cause of hypertension, estimated at 1% to 10% of the 50 million people diagnosed with high blood pressure in the United States. [1] The most common causes of hypertension are atherosclerosis or, in young women, fibromuscular dysplasia; less common causes include extrinsic compression, vasculitis, neurofibromatosis, congenital bands, and radiation. [2] Eventually, decreased perfusion can lead to structural and functional damage to the kidneys and complications of chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease. [3] Renal artery stenosis accounts for less than 1% of all cases of hypertension; however, it is a disproportionately important cause, responsible for up to 40% of cases of refractory or resistant hypertension.

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Etiology
content: Atherosclerosis accounts for approximately 90% of RAS. Atherosclerosis usually involves the aortic orifice at the proximal 2 cm of the main renal artery. This disorder is particularly common in patients with known atherosclerotic disease; however, it can also occur as a relatively isolated renal lesion. Any of the multiple renal arteries (occurring in 14%–28%) may be affected. Risk factors for atherosclerosis include hypertension, dyslipidemia, cigarette smoking, viral infection, immune injury, chronic kidney disease, and increased homocysteine levels. Diabetes and smoking cause endothelial injury, leading to plaque formation and eventually renal artery stenosis. [4] Some case reports have described stenosis of the accessory renal artery, suggesting that altered anatomy increases wall shear stress and predisposes to stenosis. [5] [6]

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Etiology
content: Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) accounts for approximately 10% to 20% of RAS. In contrast to atherosclerosis, fibromuscular dysplasia most often affects women aged 35 to 50 and typically involves the middle and distal main renal artery or the intrarenal branches. FMD usually does not cause complete lumen occlusion, unlike atherosclerotic RAS. In fibromuscular dysplasia, approximately 80% to 90% of RAS involves the tunica media at the tunica adventitia border. About 10% involves the tunica intima, and less than 5% involves the tunica adventitia. [6] [7] [8]

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Epidemiology
content: Renal artery stenosis likely affects fewer than 1% of patients with mild hypertension but may be present in 10% to 40% of those with acute, severe, or refractory hypertension, often superimposed on preexisting hypertension. Observational studies suggest that approximately 75% of cases involve unilateral rather than bilateral stenosis. [10] Studies' results suggest that ischemic nephropathy may be the cause of 5% to 22% of advanced renal disease in all patients older than 50. In fibromuscular dysplasia, involvement of the renal arteries occurs in approximately 75% to 80% of cases. Roughly two-thirds of patients have involvement of multiple renal arteries. Fibromuscular dysplasia is more common in females (~90% of cases) than in males, while atherosclerotic disease is most common in men older than 40 years. [7] [10] [11]

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Pathophysiology -- Pathogenesis of Renal Artery Stenosis
content: Evidence also indicates that adventitial and perivascular mechanisms contribute substantially to disease progression. Plaque progression may result from dysfunctional perivascular adipose tissue and vasa vasorum expansion, which release cytokines, adipokines, and extracellular vesicles that promote oxidative stress, vascular inflammation, and lesion growth. [12] Ischemic injury in RAS also activates innate immune pathways, particularly the NLRP3 inflammasome, leading to macrophage recruitment, pyroptosis, and interstitial fibrosis. Extracellular vesicles carrying microRNAs act as mediators and biomarkers of vascular and renal parenchymal injury. A heritable predisposition to abnormal arterial remodelling and shared susceptibility with spontaneous coronary artery dissection and migraine, suggested by genome-wide association studies, identified variants in the PHACTR1/EDN1 locus and other genes that regulate endothelial–smooth muscle signalling, [12] Pathogenesis of Hypertension

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Pathophysiology -- Pathogenesis of Renal Artery Stenosis
content: In atherosclerosis, endothelial injury can result from dyslipidemia, cigarette smoking, viral infection, immune injury, or elevated homocysteine levels. [13] At the lesion site, increased permeability to low-density lipoprotein and macrophage migration, along with endothelial and smooth muscle cell proliferation, ultimately lead to the formation of atherosclerotic plaque. Renal blood flow, which is significantly greater than the perfusion to other organs, along with glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure, is an important determinant of the glomerular filtration rate (GFR).

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Pathophysiology -- Pathogenesis of Renal Artery Stenosis
content: In patients with renal artery stenosis, chronic ischemia from renal blood flow obstruction leads to adaptive changes in the kidney, including the formation of collateral blood vessels and renin secretion by the juxtaglomerular apparatus. The renin enzyme maintains homeostasis in that it converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, and then angiotensin I is converted to angiotensin II by angiotensin-converting enzyme in the lungs. Angiotensin II is responsible for vasoconstriction and the release of aldosterone, which causes sodium and water retention, thus resulting in secondary hypertension or renovascular hypertension. [1] [14]

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Pathophysiology -- Pathogenesis of Chronic Renal Insufficiency
content: GFR is autoregulated by angiotensin II and other modulators between the afferent and efferent arteries. Maintenance of GFR fails when renal perfusion pressure falls below 70 to 85 mm Hg. Therefore, significant functional impairment of autoregulation, leading to decreased GFR, is unlikely to be observed unless the narrowing exceeds 50%. Studies' results demonstrate that moderate reductions in renal perfusion pressure (up to 40%) and renal blood flow (mean 30%) are associated with reduced glomerular filtration; however, tissue oxygenation in the kidney cortex and medulla can adapt without the development of severe hypoxia. Therefore, patients at an early stage can be treated with medical therapy without progressive loss of function or irreversible fibrosis in many cases, sometimes for many years.

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Pathophysiology -- Pathogenesis of Chronic Renal Insufficiency
content: More advanced stenosis, corresponding to 70% to 80% vascular occlusion, leads to demonstrable cortical hypoxia, and it is proposed that this hypoxia induces microvascular rarefaction and activates inflammatory and oxidative pathways that drive interstitial fibrosis. [15] Therefore, loss of renal function in renovascular disease, in addition to being a usually reversible consequence of antihypertensive therapy, can reflect a progressive narrowing of the renal arteries or progressive intrinsic renal disease. Eventually, long-standing parenchymal injury becomes irreversible. At this point, restoring renal blood flow does not result in recovery of renal function or clinical benefit.

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Histopathology -- Atherosclerotic Stenosis
content: The following changes occur in the intima, media, and elastic layers (internal and external elastic layers): thickening of the tunica intima layer with accumulation of foam cells, cholesterol crystals, smooth muscle cells, and inflammatory cells. The media layer becomes thin due to compressive forces from the plaque, and the internal and external elastic laminae are disrupted. [16]

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Histopathology -- Fibromuscular Dysplasia
content: Excessive fibrous tissue is deposited in the inner layer (intimal fibrosis), and thickening of the muscular layer (medial hyperplasia) is also seen. These changes result in a beaded appearance of the artery, with alternating areas of stenosis and dilatation. [17]

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- History and Physical
content: Physical examination findings may include abdominal and flank bruits. Patients with renovascular disease frequently have severe retinopathy or weak distal pulses suggestive of peripheral vascular disease. [1] [20] RAS can complicate pre-existing hypertension. In this presentation, the concern is for patients for whom RAS is complicating the management of their hypertension. Fibromuscular dysplasia often presents with neurologic signs from carotid artery involvement; suspicious findings include visual symptoms, numbness, weakness, or speech difficulties. Signs of aortic dissection are also possible, such as tearing chest pain or loss of consciousness. [21]

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Evaluation -- Laboratory Studies
content: Laboratory studies conducted in renovascular disease include the following: Serum creatinine levels are used to assess the degree of renal dysfunction. Renin and aldosterone levels are often elevated, particularly with unilateral RAS. [22] [23] A 24-hour urine collection or a protein-to-creatinine ratio in a random voided urine specimen is used to more accurately assess the severity of renal dysfunction and quantify proteinuria. Renal vascular disease is more often associated with minimal-to-moderate proteinuria, typically not in the nephrotic range. Urinalysis for red blood cells or red blood cell casts (a hallmark of glomerulonephritis) is negative. Serologic tests should be performed for systemic lupus erythematosus or vasculitis if these conditions are suspected (eg, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, C3, C4).

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Evaluation -- Imaging Studies
content: Testing for the renovascular disease is warranted in patients who fulfil the following criteria: The clinical findings suggest a cause of secondary hypertension rather than primary hypertension. Other causes of secondary hypertension, such as primary kidney disease, primary aldosteronism, or pheochromocytoma, have been excluded. A corrective intervention is planned if a clinically significant stenotic lesion is found.

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Evaluation -- Imaging Studies
content: The gold standard for diagnosing renal artery stenosis is renal arteriography. However, this is an invasive test that uses contrast, so noninvasive methods are often preferred. The choice of test should be based upon institutional expertise and patient factors. If the noninvasive test is inconclusive and the clinical suspicion remains high, conventional renal arteriography is recommended. [24] Duplex Doppler ultrasonography Computed tomographic angiography Magnetic resonance angiography [25]

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Evaluation -- Conventional Arteriography
content: As mentioned initially, conventional angiography remains the standard for confirming and identifying renal artery occlusion. There are several methods for performing renal arteriography, including conventional aortography, intravenous subtraction angiography, intra-arterial subtraction angiography, and carbon dioxide angiography. Conventional aortography produces excellent radiographic images of the renal artery but requires arterial puncture, carries a risk of thromboembolism, and requires a moderate amount of contrast, with the risk of contrast-induced acute tubular necrosis.

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Evaluation -- Conventional Arteriography
content: Low-osmolar contrast material can reduce this risk. Intravenous subtraction angiography is sensitive for identifying stenosis of the main renal artery and avoids the use of high contrast volume, the risk of arterial puncture, and arterial atherosclerotic emboli, but may not adequately demonstrate accessory or branch renal arteries. Intra-arterial digital subtraction angiography has higher diagnostic accuracy than conventional angiography and is associated with fewer complications due to a lower contrast dose and smaller catheter size. Carbon dioxide angiography is an alternative to conventional nephrotoxic contrast agents, reducing the risk in patients with severe renal disease. [24]

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Evaluation -- Duplex Doppler Ultrasonography
content: Duplex ultrasonography is a noninvasive, relatively inexpensive technique that can be used in patients with any degree of renal function. However, it is operator-dependent and has variable sensitivity. Two approaches are used to detect RAS with Doppler ultrasound.
contents: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Evaluation -- Duplex Doppler Ultrasonography. Duplex ultrasonography is a noninvasive, relatively inexpensive technique that can be used in patients with any degree of renal function. However, it is operator-dependent and has variable sensitivity. Two approaches are used to detect RAS with Doppler ultrasound.

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Evaluation -- Duplex Doppler Ultrasonography
content: 1. Direct visualisation of the Renal Arteries : The first approach involves direct scanning of the main renal arteries with colour or power Doppler ultrasound, followed by spectral analysis of renal artery flow using an anterior or anterolateral approach. Owing to various factors, particularly gas interposition and the anatomy of the left renal artery, a complete examination of both renal arteries can be achieved in 50% to 90% of cases. Signal enhancement can be achieved by administering contrast agents, which facilitate visualisation of the renal arteries. Several criteria are currently used to diagnose significant proximal stenosis: An increase in peak systolic velocity in the renal artery (the post-stenotic threshold for significant RAS is 100–200 cm/sec) A renal-to-aortic peak systolic velocity ratio of greater than 3.5 Turbulent post-stenotic flow Visualisation of the renal artery without any detectable Doppler signal, an observation that signals occlusion

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Evaluation -- Duplex Doppler Ultrasonography
content: Fasting is not necessary for renal ultrasounds, but some institutions' protocols prefer this. [24] Contrast (using microbubbles rather than iodinated contrast) may increase sensitivity, specificity, and interobserver correlation compared with Doppler ultrasound. [24] [26] Results from studies have reported that the sensitivity of this modality ranges from 88% to 96%, and its specificity is ~89%, compared with angiography. These numbers improve with severe stenosis. [24] [27]

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Evaluation -- Duplex Doppler Ultrasonography
content: 2. Analysis of Intrarenal Doppler Waveforms: The different segments of the kidneys are scanned via a transumbilical approach systematically to detect a stenosis of a segmental or accessory renal artery. Quantitative criteria  proposed for the detection of significant RAS: Early systolic acceleration is more than 350 to 400 cm/sec Acceleration time greater than 0.05 sec to 0.08 sec A change in the resistive index of greater than 5% between the right and left kidneys This value should be measured during the initial portion of the systolic rise and should exclude the late compliance peak. A dampened presentation Pulsus tardus of an intrarenal Doppler waveform indicates stenosis. The presence of an early systolic peak This can be interpreted as a sign of normality; however, the absence of an early systolic peak does not necessarily indicate stenosis. [28]

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Evaluation -- CT Angiography
content: Raw data and 3-dimensional reconstruction of the renal vascular tree are sensitive and specific methods for visualising the entire vasculature, including accessory renal arteries. Images are acquired with thin collimation and bolus tracking at the abdominal aorta. This is a useful technique because it avoids arterial catheterisation and puncture and thus reduces the risk of atheroembolism; however, it is associated with the risk of contrast-associated nephropathy, particularly in patients with pre-existing chronic kidney disease. [24] Results from studies show a reasonable correlation with angiography; one pediatric study's results reported a sensitivity of 86% and a specificity of 92%. [29]

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Evaluation -- MR Angiography
content: Different imaging methods can be used: Time of flight (TOF) in which the high velocity of the blood jet at the level of stenosis is seen as a signal void or simply black. The phase contrast technique is an imaging method that may be used. Gadolinium-enhanced MR angiography enables breath-hold 3-dimensional spoiled gradient-echo imaging with short repetition times and echo times. The angiographic contrast results from the T1-shortening effect of the intravenously administered paramagnetic contrast agent. Blood is rendered bright, whereas stationary tissues remain dark. Subtraction of nonenhanced images removes the background signal and improves the vessel-to-background contrast. Usually, a double dose of gadolinium contrast material (0.2 mmol/kg) is injected at a rate of 1.5 mL/sec to 2 mL/sec.

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Evaluation -- MR Angiography
content: According to several case studies, MR angiography has been justified only for diagnosing stenosis situated in the proximal 3 cm to 3.5 cm of renal arteries, with limited visualization of distal renal artery stenosis and segmental renal artery stenosis. In some cases, renal impairment precludes the use of contrast agents; in such cases, TOF imaging is beneficial. [25] Recently, multiparametric MR imaging can efficiently identify single renal dysfunction in kidneys with renal artery stenosis. Additionally, the cortical T1 value, combined with renal cortical blood flow, showed the highest diagnostic efficacy for renal functional impairment. [2]

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Evaluation -- Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitor Scintigraphy
content: This test measures intraglomerular pressure rather than arterial stenosis and is most accurate in patients with normal renal function (estimated at 90%), but accuracy declines significantly with decreased GFR. This test is not considered cost-effective and has been largely replaced by the other modalities described here. [30] [31] A kidney with renovascular hypertension, particularly RAS, exhibits impaired function during angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibition. This phenomenon is a manifestation of disruption of the autoregulation system of the GFR, which becomes dependent on the effect of angiotensin II on the efferent arteriole under circumstances of low perfusion.

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Evaluation -- Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitor Scintigraphy
content: Although ACE inhibition can induce a decline in GFR in the affected kidney of patients with unilateral RAS, the contralateral kidney preserves overall renal function. This change in renal function in the unilateral RAS induced by ACE inhibition can be assessed using scintigraphy. In these patients, ACE inhibitor scintigraphy induces significant changes in the time-activity curves of the affected kidney relative to baseline.

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Evaluation -- Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitor Scintigraphy
content: ACE inhibitor scintigraphy is performed 1 hour after an oral dose of 25 mg of captopril or 15 minutes after an intravenous dose of 0.04 mg/kg of enalapril maleate. Any pre-existing ACE inhibitor therapy should be discontinued 2 to 5 days before the study, depending on the drug's half-life, and adequate hydration must be ensured. Blood pressure should be monitored during the procedure. Baseline and ACE inhibitor scintigraphy is performed after intravenous injection of technetium-99m mercaptoacetyltriglycine, iodine-131 ortho-iodohippurate, or technetium-99m (Tc-99m) diethylenetriaminepentaacetic acid. Sequential images and scintigraphic curves are acquired for 30 minutes after radiotracer injection. Time-activity curves are generated from the renal cortex and pelvis. Renal uptake is measured every 1- to 2-minute intervals after injection. [30]

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Evaluation -- Summary
content: Conventional angiography is the gold standard, but it is invasive and has procedural risks. Doppler ultrasound is typically the initial test due to its accessibility, noninvasiveness, and low cost. The use of bubble contrast may significantly improve the sensitivity of this test. However, it remains operator-dependent. CT angiography shows reasonable correlation with angiography but requires iodinated contrast. MR angiography has lower sensitivity than CT angiography and is most useful for proximal stenoses (the most common) rather than distal stenoses. ACE inhibitor scintigraphy is rarely used but provides estimates of glomerular hypertension rather than anatomical stenoses, which can be useful when it is uncertain whether stenoses are incidental or functional.

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Treatment / Management -- Atherosclerotic RAS
content: Initial treatment for atherosclerotic RAS (ARAS) is generally observation instead of revascularization when the stenosis is less than 50%. The management, which involves serial control every 6 months with duplex scanning, accurate correction of dyslipidemia, and the use of drugs that block platelet aggregation, may require 3 or more different drugs to control hypertension. [32] Preferably, ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) are used for this purpose. If ACE/ARBs cannot be used, calcium channel blockers may be a suitable alternative. Strict control of serum cholesterol with statins should be achieved. [19]

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Treatment / Management -- Atherosclerotic RAS
content: The threshold for intervention in ARAS is controversial. [33] The landmark Cardiovascular Outcomes in Renal Atherosclerotic Lesions (CORAL) found no difference between medical therapy versus renal stenting in the primary outcomes of death from cardiovascular or renal causes, myocardial infarction, stroke, hospitalization for heart failure, progressive renal insufficiency, or need for dialysis at over 3.5 years. [34] Similarly, the Angioplasty and Stenting for Renal Artery Lesions (ASTRAL) trial was a randomized controlled trial comparing medical therapy with angioplasty with or without stenting in patients with moderate renal artery stenosis. This trial showed no significant difference in the rate of renal function decline, blood pressure control, mortality, or cardiovascular/renal outcomes between the two groups. Follow-up extended to ~5 years, and 23 patients had serious complications of revascularization. [35] These 2 trials suggest that optimal medical management may be equivalent to revascularization in patients without a clear indication for intervention. Most experts agree that indications for intervention in this condition are significant stenosis and one of the following: unstable angina, unexplained pulmonary edema, and hemodynamically significant ARAS with either worsening renal function or with difficult-to-control hypertension. [33]

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Treatment / Management -- Fibromuscular Dysplasia
content: Fibromuscular dysplasia responds more favorably to angioplasty than ARAS, and these patients do not require stenting. The shorter the duration of hypertension, the more likely the success rate. Approximately 20% of patients will require a repeat procedure; therefore, monitoring is crucial. Because patients with FMD often present with embolic or thromboembolic events, unless contraindicated, an antiplatelet agent such as aspirin 75 to 100 mg is recommended.

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Treatment / Management -- Fibromuscular Dysplasia
content: Catheter angiography remains the gold standard for treatment. Pressure gradients should be measured in all the lesions (as most are multifocal) to determine which are hemodynamically significant. Stenting is not advised except in the case of dissection or other complications. Rarely, surgery will be required in cases of complex lesions, aneurysms, or failed angioplasty attempts. Approximately 10% to 15% of cases may develop restenosis; however, repeat angioplasty is feasible. Despite successful radiologic outcomes, only about one-third of patients can discontinue antihypertensive medications. [9] [36]

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Differential diagnosis of renal artery stenosis includes: Acute kidney injury Primary aldosteronism Chronic glomerulonephritis Hypersensitivity nephropathy Hypertension (essential) Malignant hypertension Nephrosclerosis

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Pertinent Studies and Ongoing Trials
content: Results from recent studies have identified predictors to improve renal function after stenting. Approximately 29% reported greater than 20% improvement in estimated GFR, whereas diabetes was a negative predictor and chronic kidney disease stage 3b/4 a positive predictor of improvement. [37] In another large multicentre randomized clinical trial, the results showed no significant benefit of renal-artery stenting compared with medical management for the treatment of atherosclerotic renal-artery stenosis with respect to quality of life. [38] Renal denervation is emerging as an adjunctive treatment for renal artery stenosis in patients with uncontrolled/resistant hypertension using Ultrasonic Catheter EmitteD, The Paradise Renal Denervation (ReCor Medical), and TIVUS system (SoniVie LTD).

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Staging
content: RAS can be classified by the degree of stenosis or by the peak systolic velocity (PSV) as follows: Grade I: PSV 80 to 200 cm/s, 30% to 49% stenosis Grade II: PSV 200 to 395 cm/s, 50% to 69% stenosis Grade III: PSV more than 395 cm/s, 70 to 99% stenosis Grade IV: PSV 0 cm/s, 100% stenosis [24]

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Staging
content: Another measurement is the ratio of peak systolic volume in the aorta to peak systolic volume in the renal artery, which helps account for systemic hypertension; a ratio of 3.5 or greater suggests greater than 60% stenosis. The resistive index is an indirect measure; a difference greater than 5% between the 2 kidneys suggests unilateral disease; however, this value is specific rather than sensitive and may not be valid in older patients with underlying parenchymal disease. [39] [40]

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis of fibromuscular dysplasia is much better than that of atherosclerotic RAS. Percutaneous transluminal renal angioplasty (without stents) leads to marked improvement or cure of hypertension. Long-term progression to renal failure is uncommon. [41] Results from one study showed 39% of patients with lesions greater than 75% stenosis progressed to total occlusion within 3 to 5 years. [42] A meta-analysis of 31,689 patients (31 studies) undergoing coronary angiography found that approximately 13.4% had significant renal artery stenosis when concurrent renal artery angiography was performed. This finding highlights that renal artery assessment should be considered in unexplained hypertension undergoing coronary catherization. [43]

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Complications
content: Complications of RAS include the following: Resistant or worsening hypertension Ischemic nephropathy/progressive renal dysfunction Cardiac destabilization syndrome (flash pulmonary oedema)/ Pickering syndrome [44] [45] End-stage kidney disease Graft dysfunction in the renal transplant setting Procedural or interventional complications

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Consultations
content: Collaboration between an interventional cardiologist, a radiologist, a nephrologist and vascular surgeons is recommended.

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Serial follow-up of a patient with renal artery stenosis should include monitoring of blood pressure and renal function, along with appropriate imaging to assess disease progression. Strict adherence to medications (antihypertensives, statins, and antiplatelet agents) is essential, and cardiovascular risk modification, such as smoking cessation, weight reduction, physical activity, and sodium restriction, should be followed. [46] Patients should be instructed to report worsening hypertension, reduced urine output, or shortness of breath as soon as possible, as timely recognition and intervention are crucial to prevent further deterioration.

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: RAS is a significant and potentially reversible cause of secondary hypertension and chronic kidney disease. Early detection helps clinicians appropriately manage and prevent further progression to end-stage renal disease. Optimal patient outcomes depend on a coordinated, evidence-based approach that integrates diagnostic accuracy, risk stratification, and individualised therapy.

title: Renal Artery Stenosis -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: A multidisciplinary approach is crucial to the effective management of RAS. Primary care clinicians and nephrologists are the first to encounter the condition of patients with resistant hypertension or declining renal function. Radiologists provide decisive diagnostic insights through duplex ultrasonography, CT angiography, or MR angiography. Interventional cardiologists and vascular surgeons determine the suitability of revascularization procedures, such as angioplasty or stenting, while cardiologists also help optimise antihypertensive and lipid-lowering therapy and monitor for adverse drug effects. Nurses contribute through patient education, adherence support, and long-term monitoring. Effective communication, shared decision-making, and timely coordination among these professionals enhance diagnostic precision, ensure evidence-based management, and improve patient safety. Through structured collaboration, the interprofessional team helps achieve better blood pressure control, preserves renal function, and reduces morbidity and mortality associated with renal artery stenosis.
